extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and researchers interested in propaganda, intelligence history, and information operations
extracted.subtask_description: Encyclopedic overview of Soviet use of disinformation: its definitions, historical development (from 1923), organizational tradecraft (Dezinformatsiya, active measures, maskirovka), notable campaigns, tactics, and methods to counter it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation — Great Soviet Encyclopedia definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined in the Great Soviet Encyclopedia (1952) as "false information with the intention to deceive public opinion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an official formulation of the tactic; emphasizes intent to deceive public opinion rather than mere inaccuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation — William Safire definition
rubrics_metrics.description: William Safire wrote that disinformation was used by the KGB predecessor to indicate: "manipulation of a nation's intelligence system through the injection of credible, but misleading data".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights tradecraft element: making misleading material appear credible to manipulate intelligence ecosystems and perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and institutionalization: 'special disinformation office' / active measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of disinformation as a Soviet tactical weapon started in 1923 when a 'special disinformation office to conduct active intelligence operations' was called for; disinformation became part of Soviet political warfare called active measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames disinformation as an organized arm of state political warfare with institutional support; active measures include coordinated operations (see forgery, subversion, media manipulation). Historical note: origin dated to 1923 and repeatedly emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dezinformatsiya / Dezinformatsiya agency (black propaganda)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term dezinformatsia (dezinformatsiya) comes from a KGB black propaganda unit; a 'Dezinformatsiya agency' (reported formed in 1955) conducted black propaganda operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents the black propaganda division's modus operandi and cites that the agency placed false material in other outlets to seed disinformation; the term's origin is tied to KGB organizational tradecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dezinformatsiya agency method: planting/propagation / circular reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactic: place a false article in a left-leaning newspaper → it gets picked up by a communist periodical → eventually published by a Soviet newspaper which cites 'undisclosed individuals', thereby globally proliferating a falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit stepwise circulation technique (often called circular reporting) used to give falsehoods an appearance of independent corroboration; example and explanation attributed to former CIA director William Colby in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maskirovka — Russian military deception
rubrics_metrics.description: Soviet intelligence used the term maskirovka (Russian military deception) to refer to a combination of tactics including disinformation, simulation, camouflage, and concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions disinformation as one component within broader military deception doctrine; implies integrated multi-modal deception (not only media messaging).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgery and fake documents as covert operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of forged or falsified official documents to influence opinion and policy (examples: a falsified Presidential Review Memorandum on Africa; forged documents alleging U.S. nuclear intentions; other fake documents used to implicate the U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forged documents serve to lend apparent official legitimacy to false claims; the article cites multiple historical examples where forgeries were disseminated to influence international relations or policy debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target selection: public opinion versus decision-makers (Bittman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Official definitions emphasize public opinion as the target, but practitioners noted many operations are intended to manipulate decision-making elites and receive no publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alerts evaluators/producers that disinformation campaigns may be designed either for mass influence or for elite/targeted manipulation; success criteria differ (public uptake vs. policy/elite confusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notable campaign exemplar — Operation INFEKTION (AIDS disinformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operation INFEKTION was a Soviet disinformation campaign to influence opinion that the U.S. invented AIDS; it included allegations that the disease had been created as an 'ethnic weapon' to destroy non-whites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a canonical case study of an internationally coordinated, long-running disinformation campaign; the article notes admission by Russian foreign intelligence head Yevgeny Primakov in 1992.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notable campaign exemplar — Operation Neptune (1964)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operation Neptune (1964), designed by the Czechoslovak secret service (StB), was an elaborate operation to defame West European politicians as former Nazi collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another case illustrating use of forged/planted material to discredit political figures and influence political discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradecraft principle: seeding falsehoods to appear as legitimate reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Soviet tradecraft involved creating false stories and arranging for them to be reported as if coming from legitimate sources so the falsehood would be globally proliferated as legitimate reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual rubric for evaluating suspected disinformation: check provenance, intermediary outlets, and signs of staged sourcing; article cites multiple historical instances (e.g., planted stories, fabricated authorship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold War actors, timeline, and diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: During 1945–1989 (Cold War) disinformation was used by multiple intelligence agencies including the Soviet KGB, British SIS, and the American CIA; the word saw increased usage in the 1960s and wider purveyance by the 1980s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual criterion: when analyzing cases, situate operations in institutional and temporal context; the article gives examples of evolving scale and international adoption of techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated tactics and mechanisms (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article enumerates many tactics and mechanisms associated with disinformation and related propaganda techniques, including: astroturfing, big lie, black propaganda, circular reporting, clickbait, conspiracy theory, deepfake, denialism, fake news websites, forgery, firehose of falsehood, gaslighting, smear campaign, psychological warfare, and more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a taxonomy for recognizing production and dissemination methods; practitioners and analysts should map incidents to one or more of these tactics to understand strategy and countermeasures. The page provides many named items which can be individually investigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countering disinformation: research, literacy, fact-checking, and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods to counter disinformation listed include academic research, critical thinking, digital/media/information literacy, health literacy, fact-checking organizations, watchdog journalism, counterpropaganda, and institutional responses (e.g., CIA reports, national counter-disinformation units).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a set of evaluative and remedial measures: strengthen literacy, support fact-checking bodies, conduct academic analysis, and create institutional mechanisms to detect and respond to active measures; article lists concrete organizations and legislative responses as examples.
